comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams considering switching from Jira to Plane, possibly due to Plane's self-hosted option and free cost. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and someone would switch to take advantage of Plane's cost savings and data ownership.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira charges per user, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to own their data, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Jira has a more complex setup process, while Plane is relatively simple to set up.
* Scalability: Jira is more scalable, with built-in support for large teams, while Plane may require more configuration for large teams.
* Integration with Git: Jira has built-in integration with Git, while Plane requires a third-party plugin for Git integration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Jira
* Pros:
  + Scalable and reliable
  + Built-in integration with Git and other tools
  + Large community of users and developers
  + Robust feature set
  + Good customer support
* Cons:
  + Expensive, especially for large teams
  + Data stored on Jira's servers
  + Complex setup process
  + Limited customization options
  + Proprietary license
### Plane
* Pros:
  + Free and self-hosted
  + Teams own their data
  + Simple setup process
  + Highly customizable
  + Open-source license
* Cons:
  + Limited scalability without configuration
  + Requires third-party plugins for some integrations
  + Limited customer support
  + May require more maintenance than Jira
  + Still a relatively new tool

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large teams that need a scalable and reliable project management tool, and are willing to pay for it. Jira's built-in integration with Git and other tools, as well as its robust feature set, make it a good choice for teams that need a lot of functionality. On the other hand, Plane is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that want a free and self-hosted project management tool, and are willing to handle some of the maintenance and configuration themselves. Plane's simplicity and customizability make it a good choice for teams that want a lot of control over their tool.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Jira in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Plane server and configure it to your needs.
3. Use a third-party import tool, such as the Plane Importer, to import your data from Jira into Plane.
4. Configure any necessary integrations, such as Git integration, using third-party plugins.
5. Test your setup to make sure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of Jira. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's scalability requires configuration, which can be time-consuming and require technical expertise. However, for small to medium-sized teams that want a free and self-hosted project management tool, Plane is a good choice, and we recommend switching from Jira to Plane if you don't need Jira's advanced features and are willing to handle some of the maintenance and configuration yourself.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced features like workflow management
* Teams that want to own their data and have control over their tool
* Teams that are currently using Jira's free version and are outgrowing it
* Teams that are looking for a simple and customizable project management tool
* Teams that are on a tight budget and can't afford Jira's costs

## FAQ
### Can I use Plane for large teams?
No, Plane is not yet scalable enough for large teams without significant configuration.
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and self-hosted.
### Can I integrate Plane with Git?
Yes, but it requires a third-party plugin.
### Is Plane open-source?
Yes, Plane is open-source and licensed under the Apache 2.0 license.
### Can I import my data from Jira into Plane?
Yes, you can use a third-party import tool to import your data from Jira into Plane.
meta_description: Plane, a free self-hosted project management tool, compared to Jira. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

# Trello vs WeKan (2026)

## Overview
Trello and WeKan are project management tools that help teams organize and manage their tasks and workflows. This comparison is useful for teams considering switching from Trello to WeKan, particularly those who value data ownership and self-hosting capabilities. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration and project management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Trello offers a free plan with limited features, while WeKan is completely free and open-source.
* Data ownership: WeKan allows teams to self-host their data, giving them full control and ownership, while Trello stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Trello is generally easier to set up and use, with a more user-friendly interface, while WeKan requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: WeKan is highly scalable, as teams can host it on their own servers, while Trello's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* Integration: WeKan has a built-in calendar integration, while Trello requires a third-party power-up for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $250/month (standard plan) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1000/month (standard plan) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Trello:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Good mobile app support
* Limited features in free plan
* Data stored on proprietary servers
**WeKan:**
* Completely free and open-source
* Self-hosting capabilities for data control
* Highly scalable
* Steeper learning curve
* Limited mobile app support

## When to Choose Each
Trello is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams who need a simple, easy-to-use project management tool with a wide range of integrations. It's also a good option for teams who don't require self-hosting capabilities and are willing to pay for additional features. WeKan, on the other hand, is suitable for larger teams or organizations that require high scalability, data control, and customization. It's also a good option for teams with technical expertise who can self-host and customize the tool to their needs.

## Migration Path
1. Export Trello boards as JSON files using the Trello API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a WeKan instance on your own server or use a hosted solution.
3. Use the WeKan import tool to import the JSON files into your WeKan instance.
4. Configure WeKan to match your Trello workflow and customize as needed.
5. Test and verify that all data has been migrated correctly.

## Our Take
WeKan is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to self-host and customize. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that WeKan's mobile app support is limited, which may be a drawback for teams who rely heavily on mobile devices. However, for teams who value data control and scalability, WeKan is a good option, and we recommend switching from Trello to WeKan if you have the technical expertise and require self-hosting capabilities.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams with technical expertise who require self-hosting capabilities
* Medium-sized teams who need high scalability and data control
* Large organizations with complex workflows and customization requirements
* Teams who don't require mobile app support
* Teams who are currently paying for Trello's standard plan and can reduce costs by self-hosting WeKan

## FAQ
### Can I self-host WeKan on my own server?
Yes, WeKan is open-source and can be self-hosted on your own server. This gives you full control over your data and allows for high scalability.
### Is WeKan free?
Yes, WeKan is completely free and open-source. There are no costs associated with using the tool, although you may need to pay for server costs if you self-host.
### Can I migrate my Trello boards to WeKan?
Yes, you can migrate your Trello boards to WeKan using the Trello API or a third-party tool. WeKan also has an import tool that supports JSON files.
### Does WeKan have mobile app support?
WeKan's mobile app support is limited, but it is available. However, it may not be as comprehensive as Trello's mobile app support.
### Is WeKan suitable for small teams?
WeKan can be suitable for small teams with technical expertise who require self-hosting capabilities and high scalability. However, it may be overkill for very small teams who just need a simple project management tool.

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud

# Dropbox vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Dropbox and Nextcloud are two popular cloud storage solutions that enable users to store, share, and collaborate on files. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from a proprietary cloud storage service to a self-hosted solution, with the core use case being secure and customizable file management. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* **Cost**: Dropbox charges a monthly fee per user, while Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting.
* **Data Ownership**: Nextcloud allows users to retain full ownership and control over their data, whereas Dropbox's terms of service grant the company certain rights to user data.
* **Setup Complexity**: Nextcloud requires more technical expertise to set up and configure, especially for self-hosting, compared to Dropbox's straightforward sign-up process.
* **Scalability**: Nextcloud is highly scalable, allowing users to add storage and users as needed, while Dropbox has fixed storage limits for each plan.
* **Integration**: Nextcloud has a built-in office suite called Nextcloud Office, which integrates seamlessly with the platform, whereas Dropbox relies on third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $499.50-$829/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,998-$3,316/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Dropbox:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Robust security features
* Collaborative editing capabilities
* Limited control over data storage and ownership
**Nextcloud:**
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* High scalability and customization
* Integrated office suite and other apps
* Active community and regular updates
* Can be complex to set up and configure

## When to Choose Each
When to choose Dropbox: Dropbox is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that require a straightforward, easy-to-use cloud storage solution with a wide range of integrations. It is ideal for teams that do not require full control over their data and are willing to pay a monthly fee per user. For example, a team of 10 users who only need to store and share files, without requiring advanced customization or self-hosting, would be a good fit for Dropbox.
When to choose Nextcloud: Nextcloud is ideal for larger teams or organizations that require a high degree of customization, scalability, and control over their data. It is suitable for teams that have the technical expertise to set up and configure the platform, and are looking for a self-hosted solution that can be integrated with existing infrastructure. For instance, a team of 50 users who require advanced collaboration features, customized storage solutions, and full control over their data would benefit from using Nextcloud.

## Migration Path
1. Export your files from Dropbox in ZIP format using the Dropbox website or mobile app.
2. Set up a Nextcloud instance on your server or use a pre-configured appliance.
3. Use the Nextcloud web interface to import your ZIP file and configure your account settings.
4. Install the Nextcloud desktop client to synchronize your files across devices.
5. Configure any additional features, such as authentication or storage options, as needed.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a production-ready solution for most users, offering a high degree of customization and control over data. However, it may not be suitable for users who require a simple, hassle-free experience, as it can be complex to set up and configure. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Nextcloud's built-in office suite, Nextcloud Office, may not be as polished as some commercial alternatives. We recommend switching to Nextcloud for users who value data ownership and control, and are willing to invest time in setting up and configuring the platform. Users who prioritize ease of use and are willing to pay a monthly fee may want to stick with Dropbox.

## Who Should Switch
* Small businesses with 10-50 users who require self-hosting and customization
* Teams with specific security or compliance requirements that cannot be met by Dropbox
* Users who require advanced collaboration features, such as integrated office suites
* Organizations with existing infrastructure that can be integrated with Nextcloud
* Individuals who value data ownership and control, and are willing to invest time in setting up and configuring Nextcloud

## FAQ
### Can I use Nextcloud for free?
Yes, Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting, but you will need to cover the costs of server maintenance and storage.
### Is Nextcloud more secure than Dropbox?
Nextcloud offers advanced security features, such as end-to-end encryption and two-factor authentication, but the security of both platforms depends on the user's configuration and practices.
### Can I migrate my files from Dropbox to Nextcloud?
Yes, you can export your files from Dropbox and import them into Nextcloud using the built-in import tool.
### Does Nextcloud have a user-friendly interface?
Nextcloud's interface is functional, but may not be as polished as some commercial alternatives, such as Dropbox.
### Is Nextcloud suitable for large teams?
Yes, Nextcloud is highly scalable and can be customized to meet the needs of large teams, but it may require more technical expertise to set up and configure.
meta_description: Nextcloud, a free self-hosted cloud storage solution, offers data ownership and control. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

title: Zoom vs Jitsi Meet

# Zoom vs Jitsi Meet (2026)

## Overview
Zoom and Jitsi Meet are video conferencing tools that cater to the core use case of remote meetings and virtual events. This comparison benefits individuals and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted or open-source solution, primarily due to concerns over data ownership and cost.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Zoom offers a free plan with limited features, while Jitsi Meet is completely free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: Jitsi Meet allows users to self-host and retain full ownership of their data, whereas Zoom stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: Zoom has a more straightforward setup process, while Jitsi Meet requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Zoom is designed to handle large-scale meetings and events, while Jitsi Meet can also scale but may require more configuration.
* Screen Sharing: Zoom has more advanced screen sharing features, including the ability to share multiple screens and annotate, while Jitsi Meet's screen sharing is more basic.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Zoom | Jitsi Meet |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $13.33+/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $13.33 * 50 = $666.50/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $13.33 * 200 = $2666.00/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Zoom:**
* Easy to use and set up
* High-quality video and audio
* Advanced features like screen sharing and annotation
* Large user base and community support
* Integrates with many third-party tools
**Jitsi Meet:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for full data ownership
* Customizable and extensible
* No limits on meeting duration or participants
* Secure end-to-end encryption
However, Jitsi Meet has limitations in terms of user interface and ease of use, particularly for non-technical users.

## When to Choose Each
Zoom is suitable for teams of all sizes that require advanced features, ease of use, and a large user base. It's ideal for businesses, enterprises, and organizations that need to integrate video conferencing with other tools and services. On the other hand, Jitsi Meet is perfect for small to medium-sized teams, open-source enthusiasts, and organizations that value data ownership and self-hosting. It's also a great option for individuals and communities that require a free and customizable video conferencing solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Zoom meeting data in CSV format using the Zoom API or web portal.
2. Set up a Jitsi Meet server using a cloud provider or self-hosting on your own infrastructure.
3. Import your meeting data into Jitsi Meet using the Jitsi Meet API or a third-party import tool.
4. Configure your Jitsi Meet instance to match your Zoom setup, including settings for video quality, screen sharing, and authentication.
5. Test your Jitsi Meet setup to ensure a smooth transition for your users.

## Our Take
Jitsi Meet is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise for self-hosting and customization. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Jitsi Meet's mobile app is still in development and lacks some features compared to the web version. However, for teams that value data ownership and self-hosting, Jitsi Meet is a great option, and we recommend switching from Zoom if you have a small to medium-sized team and don't require advanced features like annotation and multiple screen sharing.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced features
* Open-source enthusiasts who value data ownership and self-hosting
* Individuals who require a free and customizable video conferencing solution
* Communities that need a secure and private video conferencing platform
* Businesses with less than 50 users that don't require integration with third-party tools

## FAQ
### Can I use Jitsi Meet for large-scale events?
Jitsi Meet can handle large-scale events, but it may require more configuration and infrastructure to ensure smooth performance.
### Is Jitsi Meet compatible with all browsers?
Jitsi Meet is compatible with most modern browsers, but it may not work seamlessly with older browsers or those with strict security settings.
### Can I integrate Jitsi Meet with my existing tools and services?
Jitsi Meet has APIs and integrations with some third-party tools, but it may not have the same level of integration as Zoom.
### Is Jitsi Meet secure and private?
Yes, Jitsi Meet offers end-to-end encryption and self-hosting options to ensure secure and private video conferencing.
### Can I use Jitsi Meet on mobile devices?
Jitsi Meet has a mobile app, but it's still in development and lacks some features compared to the web version.

title: Linear vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Linear vs Plane

## Overview

Streamlined issue tracker known for speed and keyboard-first design. is a popular proprietary tool in the project-management space. Plane is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Linear costs Free / $8/user/month; Plane is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Linear is Proprietary; Plane is Apache 2.0
- **Data ownership**: Plane can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Plane eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Plane has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Linear | Plane |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $8/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Linear

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Plane

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [makeplane/plane](https://github.com/makeplane/plane) * ~31k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Linear if:** Linear is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Plane if:** Plane is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Linear in its standard export format, review Plane import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Plane is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Linear tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Plane instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Linear, switching to self-hosted Plane will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Linear until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Linear paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Plane free to use?
Yes. Plane is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Linear to Plane?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Linear data, follow the Plane import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Plane get regular updates?
Yes. Plane has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Plane without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Plane development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Linear](https://linear.app) and [Plane](https://plane.so) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Plane is a free, self-hosted alternative to Linear. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: Microsoft Teams vs Mattermost
comparison_markdown:
# Microsoft Teams vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Microsoft Teams and Mattermost are two popular collaboration platforms designed to facilitate communication and teamwork among organizations. This comparison is beneficial for teams and businesses seeking to choose between a proprietary, cloud-based solution and a self-hosted, open-source alternative. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* **Cost**: Microsoft Teams offers a free version with limited features, while Mattermost is free and open-source, with optional paid support.
* **Data Ownership**: Microsoft Teams stores data on Microsoft's servers, whereas Mattermost allows users to host their data on their own servers.
* **Setup Complexity**: Microsoft Teams is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* **Scalability**: Microsoft Teams is designed to scale with large enterprises, while Mattermost is highly customizable and can be scaled to meet the needs of smaller teams and organizations.
* **Integration**: Microsoft Teams has native integration with Microsoft Office 365, while Mattermost has integration with a wide range of third-party tools and services through its open API.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Microsoft Teams | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $6-$22/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $6-$22/user/month (approx. $300-$1,100/month) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $6-$22/user/month (approx. $1,200-$4,400/month) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Microsoft Teams:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Native integration with Microsoft Office 365
* Scalable and reliable
* Wide range of features and tools
* Limited control over data and customization
**Mattermost:**
* Self-hosted and open-source
* Highly customizable
* Scalable and flexible
* Wide range of integrations with third-party tools
* Steeper learning curve and more complex setup

title: Google Workspace vs Nextcloud

# Google Workspace vs Nextcloud

## Overview

Google suite of cloud productivity tools including Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Meet, and Calendar. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Nextcloud is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Google Workspace costs $6-$18/user/month; Nextcloud is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Google Workspace is Proprietary; Nextcloud is AGPL 3.0
- **Data ownership**: Nextcloud can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Nextcloud eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Nextcloud has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Google Workspace | Nextcloud |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $6-$18/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$300/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,200/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Google Workspace

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Nextcloud

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [nextcloud/server](https://github.com/nextcloud/server) * ~27k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Google Workspace if:** Google Workspace is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Nextcloud if:** Nextcloud is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Google Workspace in its standard export format, review Nextcloud import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Nextcloud is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Google Workspace tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Nextcloud instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Google Workspace, switching to self-hosted Nextcloud will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Google Workspace until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Google Workspace paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Nextcloud free to use?
Yes. Nextcloud is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Google Workspace to Nextcloud?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Google Workspace data, follow the Nextcloud import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Nextcloud get regular updates?
Yes. Nextcloud has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Nextcloud without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Nextcloud development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---

Airtable and NocoDB are two popular database management tools used for organizing and tracking data. * Cost: Airtable offers a free plan and paid plans starting at $10-$20 per user per month, while NocoDB is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: NocoDB allows users to retain full ownership of their data, while Airtable's proprietary license may raise concerns about data ownership.
* Setup complexity: Airtable is generally easier to set up and use, while NocoDB requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: NocoDB is designed to scale horizontally and can handle large amounts of data, while Airtable's scalability is limited by its cloud-based architecture.
* Feature difference: NocoDB offers a built-in GraphQL API, while Airtable requires a third-party integration for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Airtable | NocoDB |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $10-$20/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $500-$1000 per month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2000-$4000 per month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Airtable:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations and templates
* Good customer support
* Limited scalability and customization options
* Proprietary license may raise concerns about data ownership
**NocoDB:**
* Self-hosted and open-source
* Highly customizable and scalable
* Retain full ownership of data
* Steeper learning curve due to technical requirements
* Limited support resources compared to Airtable

## When to Choose Each
Airtable is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams who need a easy-to-use and intuitive database solution with a wide range of integrations and templates. It is also suitable for teams who do not require a high level of customization or scalability. On the other hand, NocoDB is a good choice for larger teams or organizations who require a high level of customization and scalability, and who are comfortable with self-hosting and technical requirements.

## Migration Path
1. Export data from Airtable in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a NocoDB instance on a self-hosted server.
3. Use the NocoDB import tool to import data from the exported CSV or JSON file.
4. Configure NocoDB to match the existing Airtable setup, including tables, views, and permissions.
5. Test the migrated data and setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
NocoDB is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some features and support resources compared to Airtable. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that NocoDB requires a high level of technical expertise to self-host and configure. However, for teams who require a high level of customization and scalability, and who are comfortable with self-hosting, NocoDB is a good choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams who require a high level of customization and scalability, and do not need Airtable's integrations and templates.
* Medium-sized teams who are comfortable with self-hosting and technical requirements, and do not need Airtable's customer support.
* Large organizations who require a high level of control over their data and scalability, and do not need Airtable's ease of use.
* Teams who are already using other open-source tools and want to integrate NocoDB into their existing stack.
* Developers who want to use a self-hosted, open-source database solution for their projects.

## FAQ
### Can I use NocoDB for free?
Yes, NocoDB is free and open-source, and can be self-hosted on your own server.
### Is NocoDB compatible with Airtable templates?
No, NocoDB does not support Airtable templates directly, but you can import data from Airtable and configure NocoDB to match your existing setup.
### Can I use NocoDB with a cloud-based server?
Yes, you can use NocoDB with a cloud-based server, but you will need to configure it yourself.

Not yet, as NocoDB still requires a high level of technical expertise to self-host and configure.
### Can I migrate my data from Airtable to NocoDB?
Yes, you can export your data from Airtable in CSV or JSON format and import it into NocoDB using the import tool.
